analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA from weakening the 2024 chemical plant accident prevention rule.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 11, 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, the bill has drawn no cosponsors and no committee action since.
analysis.plain_summary: In March 2024 the EPA finalized a rule strengthening the Risk Management Program, the Clean Air Act program that requires chemical plants and refineries to prevent and prepare for accidental toxic releases. This bill would bar the EPA Administrator from proposing, finalizing, or implementing any reconsideration, revision, or replacement of that rule from enactment through January 20, 2029. In plain terms, it freezes in place the stronger safety requirements and keeps a future EPA from rolling them back.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work near chemical plants, refineries, and other facilities that handle hazardous chemicals — often called fenceline communities — along with plant workers, first responders, and nearby schools and hospitals. The 2024 rule these sponsors want to protect requires high-risk facilities to analyze safer technologies and alternatives, investigate incidents to find root causes, undergo third-party audits after serious accidents, and coordinate emergency response plans with local responders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fenceline communities, plant workers, first responders

how_it_helps.text: The bill locks in the 2024 rule 'Accidental Release Prevention Requirements: Risk Management Programs Under the Clean Air Act; Safer Communities by Chemical Accident Prevention' (89 Fed. Reg. 17622) by prohibiting the EPA from proposing, finalizing, or implementing any action to reconsider, revise, or replace it.
The protection runs from the date of enactment through January 20, 2029, covering the remainder of the current administration's term.
The bar applies notwithstanding any other provision of law, meaning the EPA could not use its normal regulatory authority to revisit the rule during that window.

analysis.who_pays: If it passes, the companies that operate covered chemical plants, refineries, and water and wastewater treatment facilities bear the cost of meeting the stronger prevention requirements — analyses of safer technologies, third-party audits, incident investigations, and emergency exercises. Some of those costs could be passed through in the price of chemicals and fuels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical plants, refineries, and treatment facilities

drawbacks.text: The rule imposes real compliance costs on facility operators — safer-technology analyses, audits, and exercises — and critics argue those costs fall hardest on smaller operators and get passed into prices for goods made with industrial chemicals.

Locking a rule in place by statute removes the usual flexibility of the regulatory process: if experience after January 2024 shows a specific requirement is unworkable or needs updating, the EPA cannot fix it until January 20, 2029, even with good reason.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a lower chance of a catastrophic chemical release, which the affected communities weigh against compliance costs borne by industry and partly passed to consumers. The 2024 rule followed serious accidents and restores requirements that were weakened in 2019; freezing it is a meaningful protection, though the statutory lock-in is blunt and prevents any mid-course correction even where one might be justified.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 11, 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote; Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Nanette Diaz Barragán introduced the bill in the House on December 11, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which holds jurisdiction over the Clean Air Act programs the bill touches.
No cosponsors have joined the bill, and no further action has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the status quo holds: the 2024 safety rule remains in effect, while facility operators keep open the possibility that the EPA will reconsider or weaken it. Because the bill has not advanced, neither communities nor industry have seen a change yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; the rule stands untouched

for.name: Rep. Nanette Diaz Barragán
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce; no other member has cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors of either party and no recorded opposition; the bill has not drawn a hearing, a vote, or a public position from either side of the aisle.

industries.note: If the bill passes, these operators lose the opportunity to have the EPA reconsider, revise, or replace the 2024 rule that tightened accident prevention requirements. Their interest in weakening those requirements runs against the safety interests of nearby residents and workers.
Refineries are covered by the Risk Management Program and would face the same frozen-in-place requirements, including safer-technology analysis and post-incident audits.

Many treatment plants use hazardous chemicals like chlorine and fall under the program; they would bear compliance costs, but freezing the rule also protects their workers and surrounding neighborhoods from accidental releases.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action in Energy and Commerce, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or a floor vote before this Congress ends; bills introduced late in a session without cosponsors almost never advance.
